# Veymark

> Per-unit identity for car parts. A cryptographic chip on the part proves itself without exposing its key, and each unit gets a passport minted on Solana. A mechanic taps the part with a phone before fitting it and sees whether it is genuine, who made it, and what is inside it — no app, no wallet, no account.

Veymark is built by two founders: one with 22 years at GM Brazil in product and materials engineering, approving parts before they went into the car; one building the cryptography and the Solana program.

Status as of October 2026: nothing has shipped. The system runs end to end on Solana devnet with 61 tests. There are no physical tags yet — a simulator produces the same SUN payloads a real NXP NTAG 424 DNA chip would, with the same cryptography and the same format. It has not been validated against physical silicon.

## The problem

Every anti-counterfeiting label in common use is visual: QR codes, serial numbers, holograms. Anything visible can be photographed and reprinted, so the defence holds until someone with a camera copies it.

When a counterfeit part fails, the manufacturer pays. They cannot prove the part did not come from their factory, so they cover the warranty on something they never made. Warranty already costs a carmaker between 2.5% and 3.5% of revenue, before counting parts that are not theirs.

Counterfeit goods account for USD 467 billion of world trade (OECD/EUIPO). In auto parts in Europe alone, EUR 4.3 billion a year.

## How it works

Three independent proofs:

- Proof of silicon. A genuine NXP chip carries a factory signature the phone verifies locally, with no server involved.
- Proof of touch. The chip emits a SUN message on every tap: UID and a read counter encrypted with AES-128, signed with a truncated CMAC. A captured payload replayed later is rejected by the counter.
- Proof in the open. Each part is minted as a compressed NFT on Solana. Anyone can read that record in a block explorer and check it against the manufacturer's public wallet.

## Sealed parts

A tag on a battery proves the case and says nothing about the cells inside. Two things answer that: the tag is applied across the opening, so opening the case tears the antenna; and the components inside carry their own tags, recorded as belonging to that case. A product declares which product fills each slot, so attaching the wrong part is refused rather than recorded.

## What Veymark does not claim

Veymark is not impossible to counterfeit, and the project does not say it is. Any verification screen can be cloned. What the chip removes is the cheap attack — photograph the label, reprint it — leaving only an expensive, traceable operation.
